name: Padded shoulders / structured jackets

lead: Pads and structured tailoring extend the shoulder line so your shoulders look broader and your torso more V-shaped, immediately. Users also say pads visually straighten sloping clavicles.

Padding sewn into a jacket, or inserts worn on the shoulder, adds volume beyond the natural frame and holds a firm outline. Fashion has used the effect repeatedly since the 1930s. No controlled studies of attractiveness effects exist; forum users report positive reactions, while others prefer building muscle.

paras: People wear jackets, blazers and coats with built-in padding and firm tailoring, or add shoulder inserts to garments. The effect is there the moment the garment goes on, and it is often paired with a fitted waist for a sharper silhouette.

No health risks were documented for fashion padding in the sources reviewed. Sports shoulder pads studied in research are a separate product. The main drawback is fit: poorly sized pads can look boxy, and the effect disappears when the jacket comes off.

angle.text: Padded shoulders and structured jackets add visible width and a more athletic silhouette the moment you put them on, with no training or surgery. Users also say pads visually straighten sloping clavicles. The look is backed by fashion history rather than attractiveness studies.

lead: Padded shoulders and structured jackets are a clothing approach used to make the shoulders look broader and the torso more V-shaped. Fashion shoulder pads are fabric-covered padding sewn inside garments to widen the shoulders and reduce the appearance of slope.[1] Because the look is created by tailoring, it changes the visible silhouette from the moment the garment goes on, with no training or procedure involved.

The idea has a long fashion history. Padded shoulders became a major women's fashion in the 1930s through Elsa Schiaparelli and Marcel Rochas, returned in the late 1970s, and defined 1980s power dressing in both women's and men's tailoring; designers such as Claude Montana, nicknamed the 'King of the Shoulder Pad', became closely identified with the shape.[1][2][3] In menswear, designers sometimes padded to create a V-shape that echoed a bodybuilder's outline.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities, padded jackets and adhesive or silicone shoulder inserts are discussed as a low-cost way to add optical shoulder width, alongside building the shoulders with training.[4][5] Research on body shape has examined the shoulders-to-waist proportions that observers rate as attractive, and fashion sources describe padding as a way to shift the silhouette toward them, but no published study has tested whether padded tailoring itself changes perceived attractiveness.[1][6]

paras: Pads inside a jacket extend the shoulder line beyond the wearer's own frame, and structured construction holds the shape. Fashion sources note that pads can also correct narrow or sloping shoulders and help heavy fabrics hold their shape [1]. This is distinct from protective sports shoulder pads, which are designed for contact sports such as American football and ice hockey [7].

Wikipedia lists several construction types. Felt-covered cotton batting was common in the 1940s and was easy to adjust but lost its shape when washed. Foam and moldable lightweight materials from 1978 onward were lighter and held their shape better, which allowed larger forms. Removable velcro-attached pads, introduced in practical form by Claire McCardell and popularised by Norma Kamali, let wearers adjust a garment or launder it without the padding. Shape variants include sharp-edged or rounded pads, pagoda shoulders and unpadded sloping cuts, and designers also used puff sleeves, tucks, pleats or flanges as alternatives to pads.[1]

In tailoring, the jacket's interlining or canvas keeps wool from stretching out of shape, with floating canvas found in expensive jackets and fused canvas in cheaper ones, which is less soft and can lose shape over time.[8] Wikipedia's suit article also contrasts the heavily padded, military-inspired cut of traditional British tailors with the less structured Neapolitan style, and notes that the American sack suit has no darts and so a straighter, looser fit.[8]

The visual effect depends on proportion. Shoulder padding raises the ratio of shoulder width to waist, which the eye reads as a more V-shaped upper body. Wikipedia's physical-attractiveness article reports that women tend to prefer men with broad shoulders, a relatively narrow waist and a V-shaped torso, citing Glassenberg and colleagues (2010) and Perrett and colleagues (1998), and that a study by Fan and colleagues (2005) found waist-to-chest ratio to be the largest determinant of male attractiveness.[6] Dixson (2003), studying women in Britain and Sri Lanka, found a waist-to-shoulder ratio of 0.6 combined with a muscular build and moderate chest hair often preferred.[6]

Those studies examined bodies and drawings, not clothing, so the contribution of padded tailoring to impressions has not been measured. Fashion history nonetheless shows designers using padding to achieve the same silhouette: a 1985 fitness craze pushed men's suits toward broader shoulders and more suppressed waists, and by 1991 shoulders had been enlarged until they resembled bodybuilders' outlines.[1]
Wearers also describe a second use. Pads can change the line of sloping shoulders, and fashion sources describe correcting narrow or sloping shoulders as one of their purposes.[1][4]

Early fashion pads were semicircular or triangular, stuffed with wool, cotton or sawdust, and used to extend the shoulder line on sleeves such as the leg-o'-mutton styles of the 1890s. Wikipedia credits a Princeton football player with inventing the athletic version in 1877, and notes that by the 1910s pads were appearing in non-athletic menswear.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, names the Princeton student as L.P. Smock and dates commercial leather pads to around 1901; it treats shoulder pads only as protective sports equipment.[7]

In 1931 Elsa Schiaparelli and Marcel Rochas introduced padded shoulders in women's wear, with Schiaparelli the designer most closely associated with the look. Influences included Southeast Asian ceremonial dress seen at the 1931 Paris Exposition Coloniale and Travis Banton's broad-shouldered costumes for Marlene Dietrich; the variety of shapes peaked around 1935 and 1936.[1] During World War II women's fashion became more militarised and pads grew bulkier and higher. Claire McCardell (1940) and Edward Molyneux (1941) removed them, and Cristobal Balenciaga (1945) and Christian Dior's 1947 New Look established a sloped, natural shoulder.[1] In menswear broad padded shoulders were common, and zoot suits exaggerated the shape.[1]

Pads gradually faded through the early 1960s, and in menswear Pierre Cardin's 1960 collection introduced slimmer, unpadded, sloping shoulders and rejected what the article calls the 'Tarzan' look.[1] Revivals began in the early 1970s with Biba and Yves Saint Laurent, and mid-decade books such as John T. Molloy's Woman's Dress for Success Book (1977) codified a structured office look.[1][2]

In fall 1978 designers worldwide embraced wide, padded shoulders, with Saint Laurent's January 1978 collection credited with launching the trend. Two versions emerged: a retro 1940s revival in Paris and a sportswear version from American and Italian designers, and public response was initially hostile.[1] In menswear Armani's mid-1970s unconstructed blazer, with sloping shoulders and little padding, gave way by 1978 and 1979 to wider, padded shoulders and narrower waists, while Cardin described his silhouette in 1979 as an upside-down triangle.[1]

Norma Kamali's 1980 sweatshirt-fabric collection, with velcro-attached removable pads, is often credited with making pads acceptable to the public, and foam pads allowed larger shapes.[1] Padded shoulders became a hallmark of power dressing, the workplace style that helped women assert authority in male-dominated settings; Margaret Thatcher is its best-known example, and Dallas and Dynasty helped popularise it.[2] Claude Montana, born in 1947 and known as the 'King of the Shoulder Pad', led the shoulder-pad movement from 1978, and his sharp silhouettes came to define the era.[3]

In menswear pads became mainstream in business suits, with jacket shapes often echoing bodybuilder physiques.[1] By 1989 retailers and the public had embraced pads, and manufacturers were producing millions weekly, according to Wikipedia's account, while in the mid-to-late 1980s some designers, such as Karl Lagerfeld, moved pads to the hips or reduced them.[1]

Pads persisted into the early 1990s, with a 1993 US patent covering a removable pad with a hidden pocket, before a backlash against 1980s styling led to smaller, subtler pads by the late 1990s.[1] Wikipedia reports a resurgence from the late 2000s, driven by 1980s nostalgia and popularised by performers such as Lady Gaga and Rihanna, and again in the late 2010s.[1] Wikipedia's suit article notes that lapels widened again in the 2020s, with the gorge and button stance still high.[8]

On looksmax.org, one user reported wearing adhesive silicone shoulder inserts and being asked whether he played football and about his workout routine; he said they also made his clavicles look straighter even though his frame was already broad [4]. Another thread asked for brand experiences and described padding as an underrated optimization when done well [5]. Some replies disagreed: one user compared inserts to a male push-up bra and said he preferred building lateral deltoids, and another suggested padding would suit only people with sloping shoulders and clavicles [5]. A third poster replied that the inserts were for military use and that needing them meant 'it's over', a common forum idiom for a perceived failure of looks [4]. These are individual reports and opinions.
Forum posters weigh padding against building lateral deltoids as ways to change shoulder width, with some describing inserts as an immediate option and others preferring muscle.[4][5]

Related approaches to a V-shaped silhouette include tailoring that suppresses the waist, structured jackets with built-up shoulder seams, and the suit styles that Wikipedia's suit article describes, from the heavily constructed British cut to the unstructured Neapolitan jacket and the dartless American sack.[8] In the 1980s the fashion V-shape was explicitly modelled on the fitness boom, linking padding to training culture.[1]

No health risks are documented for fashion padding. Adhesive inserts worn on skin are a separate category of product, and no research on their effects was found. Wikipedia notes that traditional felt-covered batting lost its shape when washed, which is why removable pads became popular for easy laundering.[1]

No studies found on padded or structured tailoring and perceived attractiveness. Published research on shoulder pads concerns protective sports equipment, such as a randomized laboratory study of ten football linemen in which wearing a full uniform including shoulder pads caused rectal temperature to rise faster and shortened treadmill time compared with a partial uniform without helmet and pads, and surveillance of football injuries [9][10]. Separate research on male body shape, including studies of waist-to-chest and waist-to-shoulder ratio, is summarised in Wikipedia's physical-attractiveness article [6].

lore.intro: Forum users describe shoulder pads and structured jackets as a cheap way to add shoulder width, with opinion divided on whether inserts are worthwhile compared with building the shoulders.[4][5]

claims.claim: Shoulder pads add visible width and a more athletic look
Pads can straighten sloping clavicles visually
Padding is a lower-effort substitute that some would drop once they can build deltoids
A broad-shouldered V-shape is what women find attractive
